Dr. Davis has to be one of the nicest professors I have ever had! He is so kind and passionate to his students and so easy to approach. In lecture, he explains things very well in a way that is easy to understand. The biggest issue I had with this class is that lectures were a bit disorganized. 
There are 4 exams, one of which is dropped, with 100 points each. He also provides 3 practice exams, which you can complete for 3 points of extra credit each. There are no other grades for this class, so you have to do well on exams in order to get a good grade.
I have to give credit to his TA, Nick, as well. I would not have gotten through the class without him. He responds to emails SO fast. His exam reviews and discussions were the only thing that got me through this class. He is the best TA I have ever had.

Dr. Davis is a remarkable professor, and Orgo II was actually my favorite class of the semester. It's just like all the other reviews mentioned. Unlike others, he keeps a steady pace, repeating concepts to cement the information and connecting concept material to real-like examples and products in nature. While the class structure is 100% exams, I felt the exams themselves weren't that difficult and could have done better. His standards are high for an A (90%+!). Regardless, Dr. Davis was a pleasure to have, and, sadly, we might not see him again for Orgo II. I wish him the best in all his future endeavors!

Dr. Davis was sociable, receptive to questions, and seemed passionate about chemistry. He explained things fairly well and connected them to real-life concepts (like common medicines, animals, etc.) His practice exams and wealth of past exams, as well as all the lecture notes being posted on Canvas, were extremely helpful. Davis also offered extra credit points before each exam and dropped our lowest exam grade.

That being said, it’s hard for me to understand why people love Davis as much as they do. His lectures felt pretty disorganized (especially compared to Hirschauer's orgo 1) and his test difficulty jumped by magnitudes after the first exam. Test questions were sometimes weirdly misleading or unrelated to lecture material. The class was entirely exam points — no homeworks or quizzes to buffer your grade. Davis also made his final cumulative for the first time this year, which seemed unnecessary. I was lucky to have some incredible TAs (shoutout to Nick and Edward) who made this otherwise okay class into a great one.

Such a nice guy!! Definitely try to take him if you can. Lectures are engaging, clear and very productive. Dr. Davis's exams did get progressively harder, but they were generally very fair. Make sure to study a lot as exams are the only grades in this class.

Be prepared to teach yourself the content. He has clicker questions which quiz you on the content that he just went over, so if you cannot learn on the spot, you are screwed. About half of the questions on exams come from previous/old midterms he has posted and the textbook additional problems. For some mechanisms he says not to refer to the textbook and his method, making it confusing to understand what he is looking for. His grading is nice where he guarantees an 80 is an A at the beginning of the semester, however, I took this when Davis was teaching and had a nice curve, dropped exams, did not give clicker questions, and gave extra credit which was infuriating knowing we had to work 10x harder with harder material. To succeed, I recommend Professor Dave explains or jOE Chem on Youtube for concepts you do not understand.

Live love davis. Coolest professor known to man. Would love to sit down get a beer and do endless mechanisms with him. Hard class, lectures are a bit disorganized, but reorganizing the content helps you study and actually figure out the material (which is hard in itself).

Someone also said this, and I agree: I feel slightly misled by past reviews. Coming off of an A in orgo 1 which I did not find difficult, orgo 2 was a whole different experience. I love Dr. Davis, he's such a sweet and good prof, but a lot of the time in lecture, he was kind of all over the place. I also feel like he took too many questions from students and it wasted a lot of time.
Otherwise, the way the class is set up is pretty nice, 4 exams total, and your lowest is dropped including the final. The cutoffs are also rly nice, 80 is an A-. There were also 9 bonus points for completion of practice exams, def do them.
However the final was incredibly difficult. All in all, be prepared to study a lot for this class. For someone who was taking PHYS161 at the same time, I needed to focus on passing that so I didn't have much time for orgo so just bear in mind that it requires a lot of time and work.

Even though I came out with a lower grade, i genuinely appreciated having a professor like Davis. His exams reflected the practice exams well enough in order to prepare for exams. Also, he drops one of 4 exams including the final, which was great. The final also was about the same difficulty as the other exams. His TAs were super helpful as well. If you put your time into the course, you’ll come out with a good grade, and should definitely pass considering a 45 is a C-
I may not be the best at organic chemistry, but I can appreciate Davis’ drive for us to do well, and the amount of resources and help he provides.

I found Orgo II with Dr. Davis to be much easier than Orgo I with Dr. Stocker. I loved Dr. Stocker as a professor, but Dr. Davis's exams were so much easier than hers. For synthesis problems or problems where you have to make the product, Dr. Davis often provides clues like the chemical formula that you can use to double-check your work. His exams are completely doable within the time limit; for the first exam, many people even finished 30 minutes early. He also drops the lowest exam and has 9 bonus points throughout the semester. Dr. Davis doesn't have any graded assignments other than the exams and bonus points, but he does post a lot of practice material. Make sure to complete the past exams he posts since they're really helpful for understanding the exam format. Some of the past exams even have a video of him going over the answers. He also posted readings and practice problems from the textbook, but I've never used them. Discussion was really helpful for nailing down the concepts from lecture. We did lots of practice problems, so I recommend going to them even though it's not required. As for lecture, Dr. Davis was a very engaging professor. He often inserts short examples of how the reactions are used in industry to synthesize different compounds. You don't have to memorize these, but they're sometimes referenced on exams. He's very thorough when explaining concepts and he posts his notes in case you miss anything. The only negative I can think of is that his teaching pace is somewhat variable. Sometimes he teaches so slow that I sit there for a few minutes doing nothing, whereas other times I'm scrambling to write everything down. My lecture time (12:30 pm) was also way behind the 8:00 am class since he frequently paused to take questions.

alright this man gets a 10/10 for personality but like a 6/10 for his teaching. class is super enjoyable because he is an entertaining little grandpa who just wants you to enjoy. the first test was mad easy and then they got progressively harder and but little was done to prepare us for the difference in difficulty. Anyway though the discussion TAs are really clutch as they fill in all the missing information from lecture that he doesn't really explain or cover. The exams are definitely thinking based so you need to make sure to understand the content rather than just memorize reactions and mechanisms. Look at the end of the day being able to drop a test including the final marks it all worth it. I would take this man again 100 times over just for that even though he isn't the best lecturer, he makes up for it in other ways and you can still do well.

Honestly, I thought I wasn't going to be able to get an A in his class, but I ended up making it happen. His exams are pretty hard, especially compared to other professors so be prepared to spend a lot of time studying for them. He recommends reading the textbook and doing the practice problems, but I didn't always have the time to do that. My advice is, if you have the time, read the textbook and do the practice problems. Some must dos in my opinion are: review all of his lecture notes before his exams (he uses a lot of examples from lecture that are tricky- you think they make sense at the time but unless you review them you won't remember on the exam, and DO THE PRACTICE EXAMS. There was one midterm exam (the 2nd one) where he told us not to look at the old exams because all the material was different, and the average was like a 50% because he had pulled basically all the material from old exams :). 

The thing that locked me in for the final was redoing my classes midterms 1,2,3 over and over until I got 100's, I read the last chapters full of new content and did those practice problems, went through his final exam review guide and made sure I understood everything, and then did as many old midterm exams as I could. Throughout the semester, I also went to discussion at least once, sometimes 2 times a week and then went to his problem solving sessions on fridays. For midterms 1,2,3 I at least worked through the reaction summaries at the back of each chapter too, which was enough to get me to a grade that was above the average, but not an A. I didn't focus on doing old exams and I think that's what got me. 

Isaacs is funny and tries to make the class fun, especially towards the middle/end of the semester. I would definitely recommend taking Isaacs if you actually want to learn orgo 2 really well, but know that this class will take up a lot of your time. At the end of the day, orgo 2 isn't meant to be easy and now I'm glad I'll know it really well for when I take the MCAT. I don't regret taking him at all

Only reason he doesn't get a 1 star is because he's a little bit better in his office hours. But overall his teaching style is very slide based. One day we had another professor cover his class and that was the most I ever learned in one of his classes. A 50% is guaranteed to be a C, so that should tell you how bad the exams are, you study for hours and days only to get a C on them which ends up not being that bad but you have barely any clue what your grade is until the end of the year. He teaches like you're on of his grad students with years of chemistry under your belt, do yourself a favor and go with another teacher if you can.

Isaacs is not the greatest at teaching the content. However, he is candid about the content of the exams. You have to do textbook problems, read nomenclature from the textbook, and do as many practice exams as possible. He provides like 10 practice exams per midterm, but none for the final. Also, the midterms and the final are very fair. The curve is 50% to 80% is a guaranteed B or C. And above 80% is a guaranteed A. I do believe he strays from the curve sometimes, but only in a way that benefits everyone.

Dr. Davis is the sweetest man who truly wants every student to do well in Orgo II. To be honest I only went to around 5 lectures over the course of the entire semester because I didn't really find them helpful (and it was an 8 AM)-- his lectures are kinda disorganized, slow-paced, and focused on the wrong things at times. I self-studied the entire course from the textbook and Dr. Davis' lecture notes (which he posts immediately after each class). Honestly I'd recommend this approach because his teaching is pretty aligned with the textbook content and the practice exams do a decent job of preparing you for exam questions. His TAs (particularly Nick) are also amazing and go out of their way to help students and hold review sessions! As for grading, Dr. Davis offers a generous curve- an A (no minus) was 90% and there was some extra credit, as well as the option to drop 1 out of 4 exams (including the final). I appreciated how quickly and transparently everything was graded and I thought the design of Dr. Davis' course is very fair and generous overall.

In my opinion, orgo 2 is a lot harder than orgo 1. The only difference is that you’re already exposed to the material so you probably figured out how to study for the class. That being said, no matter which professor you get, you’re going to have to study a lot regardless. Isaacs reuses a lot of questions from practice exams (which he gives you all the way back from 2011), or will change questions to require the same/near identical steps. I still recommend watching additional youtube videos on content and practice problems (my favorite are That Organic Chemistry Tutor and Organic Chemistry with Victor). 80% or higher is a guaranteed A-/A/A+ and I got an 85% which was marked as an A. Make sure to stay on top of studying because clicker questions in class are partially graded on accuracy. If Davis is available, I’d say you’re better off getting an A with him but I still found Isaacs to be a really great professor.

I honestly cannot believe I got an A in this course. I remember being so terrified the first week of classes because he started lecturing on the first day and I was already lost and all of my friends had Davis so I was freaking out. The night before the first midterm I literally considered withdrawing (thankfully I didn't). However, I grew to love his teaching style and found his lectures to be interesting. Isaacs is very passionate about organic chemistry and it definitely helped me stay focused during the 75 minute lectures. He can be pretty cold at times but he tends to throw in a few jokes when lecturing which lightens the mood. I've heard he's not the most helpful at office hours but I never went lol. You have to go to lecture for the clicker questions, and honestly if you don't go you will be very lost. I only missed maybe 4 lectures the whole semester and I felt it set me behind when studying. He included about 100 points of clicker questions, which were graded half for accuracy and half for trying. Each midterm was 200 points and the final was 300 points. There are no homeworks so no buffer. Averages were in the 50s-60s and the curve was pretty decent. I had about an 80 in the class, scoring roughly 70s and 80s on the midterms and final, and ended with an A (he guarantees that if you get at least an 80 you will have an A). I was hoping his curve would be a little bigger, sometimes he changes it, but I guess not last semester. His notes are very difficult to read and follow along with after lecture so I tended to mostly use the textbook and took notes on each topic to study. Sometimes the textbook uses different mechanisms than he teaches so make sure to double check things. He included 10+ previous exams WITH answer keys for each midterm which was extremely helpful. 

Here are my tips for success:

-Start studying at LEAST a week before the exam. You can't cram for this class.
-Go to discussion and ask questions. I absolutely loved our TA he was amazing and so helpful.
-Take notes on the textbook to study. Do all of the practice problems at the bottom of the page.
-If you can come up with your own practice problem or explain it to someone else, you probably know the material.
-Learn all of the mechanisms for each reaction and make sure you can replicate them.
-STUDY OLD EXAMS. This is absolutely key to success. The questions he uses on exams are very similar conceptually to old exams and sometimes even the exact same.
-Don't forget about nomenclature. These are freebies on the exams if you study these. Make a quizlet and just go over them once a day if you can.
-Go to GSS and office hours. Tbh I never went but I always attended the exam reviews from the GSS leader. I also did his worksheets from the sessions to study.

GOOD LUCK!

Good: Very nice and makes class fun (I saw him one day passing at Mogee Tea and bro came up to me and gave me a fistbump), drops 1 exam including final and aren't too hard (as someone coming from Baxter and Stocker), practice exams very similar to real exams, overall anything you will need to know will have been on the lecture slides that he posts, 9 EXTRA POINTS for a class out of 300 points total.

Bad: Probably have retired by the time you read this, teaching style a bit rough to follow and a disorganized, you will need to look up stuff after class and teach yourself a bit. 

Overall if he hasn't retired: take him

The first day of lectures she told us she prided herself on being apathetic. Does not care to help students. Hands out 0s like candy. No partial credit on pages of mechanisms. Yaps all lecture long and none of it pertained to the homework or tests. I should have withdrawn while I had the chance.

Davis is such a nice guy, but honestly a very mid teacher. The way he taught didn't really make sense and the best way to learn was through the discussion where the TA would go over every mechanism we needed to know. The exams fortunately were quite easy but on very random topics so it was difficult to study for them and required you to rely on intuition most of the time. The best part about this class is that one exam which include the final can be dropped. Overall, easy class but mid teacher.

Davis is a really nice guy, I didn’t get to know him very well but in lectures he seems very supportive and doesn’t hesitate to take up class time answering everyone’s questions. That being said, I felt very unprepared for all of his exams because it was so hard to learn from his lectures. Though he’s a great person, it was hard to stay awake in his class and maybe it’s just a me thing, but I had to fight tooth and nail to get an A- lol. 

The structure of the class is very straightforward, but thats also a negative because he has no support to help your grade other than 9 extra credit points which didn’t do much for me in the span of things even when I did all of the extra credit. The total points for the class when I took it was 300, and each exam is 100 points so he drops the lowest and you can add 9 to get a max of 309/300 if you’re a genius. The first exam was very straightforward, but I’d recommend to never take any of his exams for granted and study until you feel very prepared because only the exams make up the grade. I originally took this class because I heard his exams are really easy and he teaches well so you are prepared, but I realized it was the total opposite after the second exam. I think maybe in his last classes the exams were easier but definitely not for my class. His form of homework is textbook problems, but they aren’t assigned or graded. I’d recommend paying attention to what he says in class because he focuses more on application and chemical kinetics than mechanisms, so focus on why specific reactions happen while you memorize them, since both are tested. 

A few people in my class did get very good grades, so it’s very possible, but if you have a packed semester with a bunch of other classes its very hard to prioritize his class. Also by the time you read this he may have already retired lol.

Has a very old style teaching. Literally just lectures in class, he seems very passionate about what he does however the class only has exams no homework.  And our class average was so low, however he wont drop nor curve. Only take if he is the ONLY option, otherwise just postpone to next semester. As well as the TA, he seems like a nice guy however his teaching style was not suitable for anyone.

Had him for orgo 1 and 2. He is so nice, has fantastic notes and lectures, and incredibly difficult exams. But they are curved so its fine. All orgo classes are hard. remember that resonance is always the answer.

Exams:

They are the same exact format (some problems even copy paste), but with different reagents, etc. The exams are not meant to be hard, he doesnt try and trick you, its all very straight up, you just need to make sure you memorize a lot of the content at least a week prior to the exam. That was long, but overall I wouldnt say this is an "easy A", but maybe an easier A compared to the other teachers (unless its davis lol). You will definitely learn a lot in this class though. dont be discouraged if you have to end up taking him, i would take him again

I had Dr. Stocker for both orgo 1 & 2. She's pretty straightforward when it comes to teaching the material and what her expectations are for you in terms of content you need to know for exams.  She writes fast (be prepared to take pictures of some of the slides she writes on otherwise you might miss important information because it's hard to keep up with her). This review may sound like just another angry student coping with their poor performance in a class. I originally had Davis, but he must have gotten snapped out of existence by Thanos over break because he disappeared and was replaced by Dixon. Davis is by far the best Orgo professor at UMD, but this isn't a Davis review so more about Dixon:

I would rather be the 1000th person in Bonnie Blue's hotel room than in Bonnie Dixon's 241 class again. Dixon is one of the best you could get. Some of the complaints I’ve seen are valid, but overall, she really sets everyone up for success, you just have to put in the work. Her teaching is super straightforward, and honestly, you couldn't ask for a better professor when it comes to explaining difficult concepts. She made Orgo I material so clear that applied to Orgo II, I wish I’d had her for Orgo I too. She gives you everything you need to complete the homework, but just a heads-up: the homework is hard and takes hours. Still, I’m so thankful for it because it made me interact with the material and constantly ask questions, which helped me learn. I took Orgo II with a different professor before and had to withdraw, so I really appreciated how much Dixon’s homework pushed me to understand the content. 

I went to her office hours at least twice a week and never found her rude or condescending. She was always encouraging, told me I was doing well, gave me helpful hints when I got stuck, and would even teach shortcuts. After spending so much time in her office, I get why some students might think she’s a little harsh, but a lot of it depends on how you approach her. If you show up without trying the problem or just want her to give you the answer, she’s not going to respond well. She can definitely tell who’s done the work and who hasn’t. Doing well on the homework really sets you up for success on the exams so do not just copy answers from someone. The homework is often harder than the exams, which is a good thing. The exams are very fair, and she’ll often tell you exactly what to expect, she’s super transparent.

She also offers extra credit, which can be a bit of a trap if you’re not careful. Definitely do it, but don’t let it take priority over studying for the exam. It’s time-consuming, but worth it if you manage your time. I wouldn’t spend more than two days on it. Her weekly review sessions are basically extra lectures, but they’re super helpful and usually align directly with the homework. It’s a little annoying that she doesn’t let you into the Zoom late, but they’re recorded, so it’s not a big deal. The final was really fair, and again, she told us exactly what to expect. Between all the resources she provides, her help in office hours, and Nick (the best TA ever), this class is totally doable.

If you don’t have a lot of time to commit, you might want to take the class with someone else. But if you genuinely want to learn and feel confident in Orgo, Dr. Dixon is the best professor you could ask for.

Honestly, Dr. Dixon is an incredible professor. Did I almost cry before every exam from feeling overwhelmed? Yes. But she genuinely sets you up for success, and her exams are never curveballs. They’re designed to test how well you truly understand the material—not to trick you.

Like many others have said, you do need to go to office hours regularly (I went MWF and had lectures on TuTh), but it’s absolutely worth it. Somehow, I ended up with an A—even though I had withdrawn from Orgo I just a year ago (but that’s a story for another time).

My advice: don’t take her attitude personally. Stay focused, do the work, and you’ll find a lot of amazing people in the same boat as you. Also, huge shoutout to Nick Simms—he’s fantastic. Oh, and one last tip: make sure you’ve memorized all the reactions from Orgo I... because there are at least 50 more waiting for you in Orgo II lol. 

Good luck everyone!!!

This class (CHEM241) was difficult but incredibly rewarding.  Organic chemistry is a hard subject because it is very different from other classes.  You can't memorize or cram and expect to be successful.  But if you're reading this review, chances are you have to take ochem regardless.  And also, odds are this isn't the last chem class you're going to have to take.  TLDR, if you want to make the most of organic chemistry and be prepared for future courses, take Dr Dixon.  

I took this course in Spring of 2025.  Originally I had registered for the TuTh 8am section because it was supposed to be with Dr Davis, and then it was switched to Dr Dixon.  I had heard horror stories about her previously so I was honestly scared for the impending semester.  However, I was happily surprised by Dixons orgo 2 class.  (On the last day of lecture, she said "I know I'm not who you wanted to have, but I still hope you enjoyed learning about chemistry this semester," which to be completely honest made me tear up ;) 

I strongly feel that Dr Dixon sets students up for success.  She lives and breathes UMD chem.  Even though she taught 3 large chem classes this semester, she still made plenty of time for our class.  Her office hours are essentially open every day 8am-2pm, except for when she is lecturing of course.  She also provides CAN (chemistry at night) which is a gold mine of practice problems which are usually helpful for/closely related to the homeworks.  Homeworks are often graded with in a day or two, and exams are graded quickly as well.  For one of the midterms, we took it at 8am and I had my grade the same day before 3pm.  Unlike other chem professors, Dixon doesn't do chem research, which I think helps.  She really is just here to teach, and she loves doing it.  

Homeworks are difficult.  But by going to every lecture, and either attending CAN or watching the recording, they are doable.  I didn't go to discussion because of my job (I did the practice problems though) and I went to office hours maybe 2 or 3 times the whole semester when I was just completely stuck on the HW.  Exams are also tough, but they are very similar to the HWs.  Also, she often outlines what will be on each exam.  One thing I love is that there is so much opportunity for extra credit.  Each exam is out of 100 pts, but there are around 110 points available on each exam.  There is also (time-consuming) extra credit which can be done beforehand and added to the score.  The exam score will not go over 100 though.  But this definitely helped me be less anxious about the exams, because I know I can skip something and still do well.  

Personality wise, I think Dr Dixon is hilarious.  One day she was playing music loudly when we came in at 8am.  She also makes jokes and sometimes talks about her personal life in a humorous way.  I didn't find her passive aggressive but also I don't take things personally.  I did not get bored in her lectures.  I think that all in all, she really just loves chemistry and wants to make it accessible for her students, while instilling in them the value of perseverance and strong work ethic.

Honestly not as bad as the reviews make him seem. His exams are as hard as the other reviews have said but if you study properly you can do well on them. My 69.22% was curved to a B+ I probably could have gotten an A if I hadn't failed the first exam so badly.

On the first midterm I mostly studied using the textbook practice problems but the level of the practice problems in the textbook aren't nearly hard enough to prepare you for the midterm. 

How I changed my study habits:

To prep for the final just study your midterms, the midterms from the past 3 years, and the final exam review sheet that he posts on elms and goes over during class.

Okay, here's the tea sis:

I hate her teaching style and I don't really like her vibes either. She gives off an unapproachable energy, and kind of assumes everyone is pre-med? She had some good explanations, but I missed most of them since I was catching up on the mechanism. Grade is entirely based on exams. Synthesis, mechanisms, and NMR are a lot of the exam. Requires memorization of IR, HNMR, pKas. Curve is good? Discussion is sort of helpful. GSS was my saving grace. Thank you Sophia.

Pros:
- Decent curve, minimum of 5%. 
- Lots of practice exams (only 2 with keys) and practice problems. GSS provides an extra practice exam with key.
- There was this one time she explained her "little hints" that really made understanding synthesis click for me.
- Gives little tricks and theoretical notes that are helpful to understanding mechanisms

Cons:
- YOU CAN'T GET THOSE LITTLE TRICKS AND NOTES UNLESS YOU'RE KEEPING UP WITH HER CRAZY FAST WRITING.
- She moves very fast. With orgo 2 being so reaction based, a lot of time is spent copying down mechanisms. It's really easy to fall behind with how fast she moves, which means you can miss all of the helpful theory she talks about. Be prepared to take a lot of pictures if you can't write fast.
- Sometimes skips steps (mostly proton transfer) in mechanisms, even though you're expected to write out all the steps on the exams.

- Entire grade is based on exams.
- Practice midterms greatly vary in difficulty. Practice problems are easier than the exams, and homework problems are supposedly harder. Most of the homework is also distractingly watermarked.

The only reason she isn't 1 star is because her explanations are sometimes good and her little hints for synthesis are good. Shame I missed nearly all of them and so will most people.

Overall, I would take her over any professor, and you are doing yourself a disservice if you choose anyone else to take.

Had for orgo 1 and 2 (1 in spring, 2 in summer). Class is hard but interesting. A shame bc I find it interesting but literally struggle so hard to barely pass. I would feel good on PP sets then bomb and exam. Felt like her final exam format was a throw off and overall unfair as literally the entire class ran out of time on the exam. Curve seemed to be ~10 points as a low 60’s is a C-. But since I took in the summer not sure how different the outcome would’ve been during a 15 week vs 6 week. I like her notes sheets and pp sets, just wish the exam formats were more consistent and achievable in a timely manner.

Just terrible. Exams were hard, but no problem sets were offered to help test your knowledge and help your overall grade. Everything in this course is essentially self-taught. He would be incredibly condescending if you asked a question.

Do not take this Professor unless you want to teach the entire course to yourself. He said everyone who got the average on midterm one is in the danger zone of failing the class. He does not teach anything!!

Dr. Isaacs is a nice guy, he is really friendly. However he doesn't teach you didly squat. He literally reads off his premade slides and doesn't do any practice with you. The literal only way you could suceed is going to his problem sessions, but I couldn't go because of class. It is so hard to focus in his class because he just drones. When I was reading these reviews and was like "oh I can power through, orgo 2 is just a hard class." No, head the warnings. HEAD MY WARNING. I got a B in orgo 1 and I failed his first exam because the questions were so difficult. Some of them he pulls from old exams, but they are nothing compared to other professors. He published a histogram at the end of exam 1 and the majority of students were in the "danger column." I counted and 95 people were either "in danger" or he recommended dropping the course, and 115 were passing. I professor should never get a 50% as an average and be able to keep their job. If you can, just wait a semester if he is the only one available. Or, honestly, take chem over the summer because that's when the good professors teach.

Going into this class, I thought that I would have a great experience since I have always heard other people praising and glazing this professor back and forth and it was extremely hard to get him (I had to keep on refreshing on Testudo). But, ever since I have had him, I swear I have had the opposite experience that other people had. Maybe he was great before (with his exams) but I feel like this semester he has changed and made the exams even more harder, in comparison to old exams he posted onto Canvas. He even says that there is no curve and that he isn't adjusting the curve this semester when even though for our past two exams, the class averages weren't great. It is actually crazy how you need a 90% to get an A in this course when for the past two exams, no one has gotten a 100%. I don't even know what my grade will end up being because of the fact that he isn't adjusting the curve. Just remember, that you might not have a wonderful experience going into this class and don't rely solely on these positive reviews. Although he is a great instructor, his newer exams don't reflect that.

Genuinely honored to have the most organized professor ever. Gives you predetermined grade cutoffs at the beginning of the semester so you don't have to overthink (80 for an A-) and he outlines the topics you need to know for exams. Exams rely on intuition but are generally fair if you study the material. As most people have said, you can drop the final exam if do good on the first 3 exams (there's 4 exams total and he drops 1). He's old, but I hope this guy never retires

Honestly, lectures were hard to follow - but exams werent that bad. I do think his exams were easier in past semesters. Five stars because you can drop an exam (crazy for a chemistry class). If you arent super passionate about chemistry and want the easier A... take Davis!!!

Get ready to teach yourselves and cry :)
It's not impossible to succeed, but you can NOT rely on the professor to help get you there.
It's going to take countless hours of self-teaching, studying, YouTube videos, GSS, TA's, peers, and maybe even tutoring.
If you like Orgo and enjoy studying, I'm sure you'll do okay, but for me, I've hated every second that I've dedicated to that class (and there's been a lot of them, best believe)
I'm going to give you a pros and cons list now so you can see the full picture... (keep in mind, this WILL be a hard class no matter who you take it with)
PROS: 
He gives past exams that are the exact same format as the actual exam
He tells you what problems from the textbook to do
You don't need to name any compounds (only draw them)
HUGE curve!!!! (80% for a flat A and 50% for a C)
You don't have to do any homework or turn anything in, ever
CONS:
Exams are crazy hard (50% averages)
He emphasizes memorization rather than understanding concepts and there is way too much to actually memorize
He grades harshly and takes more points off than I think is necessary
His notes are really unorganized and hard to follow
His lectures are really boring

Final verdict is if I could take this with someone else I would, and I hated it so bad, but I guess it really could have been worse, and I promise you'll be fine

His lectures are just reading off of slides and regurgitating the textbook. It's better to learn on your own. Professor Wang is a good person and cares about his students. I might just be dumb and refused to study... Speaking in hindsight, consistency is key and his practice exams are 95% similar to his actual exams. He also has guaranteed synthesis problems that he'll cover in lecture before exams. Good luck! I hope I pass.

He's ok but not a first choice for orgo 2. He just has premade slides that go along with the textbook (free). Just read the textbook and do those practice problems (especially the ones he mentions in the syllabus as he has pulled questions directly from there). It will be more than what you get out of going to his class. I passed the first two exams (with a 66% and 62%) and got a 40% on the final (MCQ for F25). He posts old exams which are helpful but does not post much (if anything) for the final. I am just happy to pass the class, but if you have a choice, take someone else.

People have given this man too much credit. This is his last semester teaching, because he is retiring next semester. I am sure he was an amazing lecturer, but this semester the lectures were just so hard to understand, and I felt like I didn't learn anything until I found online resources. His exams are confusing, but he leaves lots of breadcrumbs and hints to help you along. His cutoffs are good, and it is very easy to not fail, but very hard to do well. For a professor who is supposed to be the easy one, our averages were lower than Isaacs exam once. He also puts lots of true/false on the exam, which just doesn't belong on an orgo exam, because there is not a lot of partial credit. If he teaches again, make sure you are consistently practicing every night, because otherwise you will not understand anything when the exams come. He is also obsessed with taking breaks and explaining real life examples of biological molecules, which wouldn't be a bad thing, except we actually need to get through content and learn. Yeah, I am sure he used to be amazing, but this semester he was not.

I have seen the greatest minds of our time crumble before organic chemistry 2. Dr. Wang is like an okay teacher I feel like it's just that the course is really hard and I feel like he doesn't give nearly enough practice. He does provide optional ungraded homeworks, but they are not representative of the test. The practice exam was the only real practice, and I feel like the homework was a waste of time. Orgo2 is the hardest course I have ever taken in my entire life, but I still think Dr. Wang isn't that bad I just think the course is evil. From what I've heard, Isaacs and Davis were worse somehow? It's hard to fathom but I believe it. Should I even be passing? I don't know. I don't even think I learned anything all semester. Also, 2 exams and a final are the only grades! This is psychological TORTURE. Imagine your entire grade hinging on each test. Horrible.

Wonderful professor. I'd be delighted to take another course with this guy. Dr. Wang cares for his students, and makes effort to get to know those who interact with him. Organic chemistry is a difficult subject, this class takes a lot of work. He provides resources that make it doable. He provides one practice exam for each ones, and our class got him to make a practice final which was a shortened version of the final. Pretty similar! Exams are usually composed of both multiple choice (usually concerning the aspects of the compound) and then free response for synthesis and mechanisms.

Unfortunately your grade is determined solely by two exams and the final. I believe it was 150, 150, and 250 respectively. An 80% is a guaranteed A- , the rest is determined by class averages. To prepare, I'd recommend doing the homework each week. Orgo 2 is jam packed with reactions so I'd really recommend reading the chapter associated with each lecture beforehand and using lecture to really hammer down the material and understand any additional info that's not in the textbook. The time I did do that, lecture and learning became more manageable. If you have the time, definitely keep up with the homework that's assigned. I didn't do all of them because it was optional so there wasn't much incentive, but when I used it to practice it was helpful. 

This class is a lot of studying and practice no matter the lecturer you take. I'd definitely recommend Dr. Wang though. Best of luck!!

Dr. Wang is one of the sweetest professors I've had at UMD. He genuinely cares about his students, and always spends time encouraging the class. I would consider the material on the exam to be fair. As previous reviews have said, he doesn't really throw hard curveballs but you do need to really understand the reactions. Grade includes 2 midterms worth 150 points each and the final worth 250 (no more clickers). Exams are structured with a nomenclature page, reactions, and at least 2 synthesis problems. He assigns ungraded homework problems but honestly I didn't really do them. My biggest suggestion would be to go to class (because he'll hint at what kind of material is on the exam, such as the synthesis questions!), and study ahead of time. Orgo 2 is hard but definitely doable.

Dr. Wang was a perfectly average professor. He mostly lectures from slides, but occasionally would write out a synthesis or mechanism. He wasn't great at explaining topics, but was good enough you could generally understand what's happening.

Pros:
- Exams were exactly like the practice exams he provided (sometimes even using the same questions).
- He gave us a synthesis during lecture, told us it would be on the exam, and it was exactly the same. He did a similar thing for the final.

Cons:
- Started an exam review saying we could ask any questions we had, and then immediately refused to answer someone's question because he already answered it in the PREVIOUS lecture.
- Not approachable if you have questions/go to his office hours.
- Homeworks are long and can be helpful, but generally that style of question isn't what's on his exams.

Overall far from the worst professor you can get. Orgo 2 is a difficult class no matter who teaches it, so make sure you spend time doing the homeworks (even if they aren't graded) and go to discussion.
This goat gave me a free A. Womp womp to the people who cannot take him next semester.

So unexpectedly evil and lazy, every time a new unit pops on the slides, the first thing you see is "nomenclature, read it yourself" except the nomenclature on the exam aren't traditional nomenclature but random niche molecules that he randomly put in slides. Also the first exam, he basically made an announcement that 50% of the class was in the danger zone of not passing with the average being like a 53%.

Davis's lectures could be a little disorganized, but he always posted annotated notes afterward. He was very easy to access by email and willing to accommodate for his lack of office hours (only once a week for a brief time). However, my grievance with this class would be that the only grades are exam grades. His exams are usually pretty fair; however, this semester, his exam averages were a little low. Primarily, this is a problem if you're a bad/anxious test-taker, because your performance on exams makes up the entirety of your grade. Davis is a very kind professor who does a good job at not making you feel bad for not understanding course content, but if you know you have a hard time taking tests, I would suggest exploring other options. Additionally, his course cut-offs are a little strange; for example, there was a 10% gap between what was an A- and what was an A, and a 12% gap between what was a C and what was a C+. Overall, he is definitely one of the best professors in the department, but it is important to take into account class style (and what makes up the grades) and finding what would work best for you as a student. I don't think the grades being made up of solely exams worked great for me, but it may be good for people who are good at self-studying and are looking to not do too much work outside of studying for the exams.

Orgo 2 is not supposed to be an easy class, but Dr. Isaacs makes it quite insufferable and extremely more difficult than it needs to be. His lecture notes are an absolute mess, and he points out that anything in the textbook is all fair game for the exam. I found that reading the textbook chapters side-by-side with his lecture notes helped me really understand the material, and before each exam I would just make a huge list of all the useful reactions with their reagents and starting/ending product. It is true that you are teaching yourself this whole class. Trying to understand why each reaction happens was just impossible and inefficient for my brain. My biggest tip is to memorize all the reactions and prioritize learning only a few important mechanisms. It is kind of frustrating because on the exams (like reaction boxes and synthesis questions) there were specific reagents you had to know that gave you certain niche products, so you had to know every reaction. Overall, the curve is very generous considering his class average is around the 50s. I got an A in Orgo 1 and also managed getting an A in Orgo 2 with Isaacs (I had a 79%). I would begin reading the textbook and taking notes two weeks before the exam. Within the last week, I was doing his textbook recommended problems and old practice exams (these are super super helpful). If you put the work in, you are capable of scoring at least average based on pure memorization.

Learning the material based off of lecture is insufficient/ineffective. Go to GSS and discussion and keep up with problems and you will be in the right state of mind for the exam. Make sure to do the practice exams as they are similar to the actual exam. Dr Issacs is very kind, however I didn't really find his lectures to be helpful. Get comfortable with the reactions for each exam and you will be in good shape.

TLDR: Not the worst, and you can do well in the class, but this would not be my first choice as a prospective orgo student.
Dr. Wang can be difficult to follow in the lectures, and the 2 midterm 1 final format can be tedious, but the practice exams give a really strong idea of what to expect on the midterms/finals, so definitely use that as your main study source. The curve Fall25 was around 65% B-, and 80% for an A-, and without a curve was a bit difficult, but certainly doable. Also, be wary of asking dumb questions in class because this mf will torch you in front of everyone. He is a nice guy to talk to in office hours, so definitely make an effort to go to them.

this was his last semester teaching so my rating wont exactly be impacting any future students, but Jeff Davis was a great professor. I once heard someone say, he'll blabber for most of the lecture, but for 10, maybe 15 minutes, it'll be liquid gold. Jeff Davis is the man to see if you want to really know, because anything you may want to know, he has known it and will let you know of it. 
4 Exams total of equal weight. Few 3 point extra credit point assignments, no other grades.
The fourth one is a cumulative final with a slight emphasis on the content in the last couple weeks of the course. 
First three are like unit exams with completely new content. 
Really nice guy. Very lucky to have caught him. Very good anecdotes too.

Yes Dr. Isaacs is a good person but his teaching abilities are okay, mediocre at best. Most of your learning will have to be from the textbook, which for me was very difficult. He barely does any practice questions in class just the one on his premade slides which I felt was never as hard as the questions on the exams. The best way to study imo is to read the whole textbook and pray for the best. The averages on exams were around 42-60%. I ended with a 60.67% which ended up being a B. Yes the curve is nice but try to avoid him if you can, unless you have many hours in your week to sit down and do every single textbook question. I honestly had a good shot at getting an A but the final exam was all MCQs (his first time doing that) and it was diabolical since no half credit. He thought that making his final all multiple choice would be easy for everyone but it was the opposite.  Nothing could have prepared me for that exam, even the 50+ hours i spent in mckeldin.  
That being said, discussion section and review sessions with the TA Nick saved me so go to those. Only take Isaacs if you know you have time to read the textbook, otherwise save your time and pick someone else if doable.

Dr. Davis is a great guy and I like the set up of his grading and curve. Allows you to drop one exam and has 3 (3 pt) extra credit practice exams. Grades are based on 3 exams (and the extra credit) and you can even drop the final. I sort of wish he assigned more structured homework as I didn't really find the textbook all that helpful. I also didn't really like his exams, there was a lot of multiple choice, fill in the blank, and true or false. If you're good at these kinds of questions, take Davis. I had Koppel for orgo 1 and did so much better on her exams and in her class overall since it was very mechanisms based and gave a lot of partial credit.

Going into this class, I had heard a lot of positive reviews about Dr. Davis, and I also had a strong chemistry background (all As up to that point). First off, Dr. Davis is incredibly kind—honestly one of the nicest professors I’ve ever had. He explains concepts clearly, takes time during lecture to answer student questions, and you can tell he’s an expert in his field. That said, the class itself is somewhat disorganized. His notes aren’t great, and lectures can feel scattered. At times, he would lose his train of thought and jump to a new topic unexpectedly. On top of that, the class meets at 8 frickin AM, which made it so cheeks to attend, so I stopped going after the first couple of weeks. In terms of grading, your final grade is almost entirely based on exams, which is pretty standard for chemistry courses. The best part about Dr. Davis’s grading policy is that he allows you to drop one exam—including the final. The exams themselves are fair, and if you understand the material and complete the practice exams, you should be in good shape. The first midterm is very easy, and you should absolutely take advantage of it to buffer your grade. The only reason I earned an A in this class was because I did extremely well on the first exam. The second exam was by far the hardest for me, mainly because I wasn’t prepared for the jump in difficulty. Each exam gets progressively harder, so you definitely need to increase your studying as the semester goes on. The second exam ended up being my dropped exam. The third exam and the final were similar in difficulty, and I scored in the top 25% of my class. Dr. Davis also offers bonus points for completing practice exams—nine points total, with three points per midterm. I initially thought I would receive an A− since I narrowly missed the 90% cutoff, but Dr. Davis adjusted the grading cutoffs after the final, which ultimately earned me an A. For studying, I started about three days before each exam. I made a review packet based on his in-class notes (which was often my first real exposure to the material since I wasn’t attending lecture), made sure I fully understood the concepts, memorized key information, and completed two to three practice exams. If I could do it again, I would definitely make time to complete more of the practice exams to feel more confident going into the tests.

Here's the thing the difficulty of this class depends on how much you keep yourself accountable. There's only 2 midterms and a final so there's not much work for this class but if you want to do well you need to spend a good amount of time every week learning and understanding the material. Personally I did not spend as much time on this class than I should have and that's because the structure of Isaacs class made me unmotivated. Lectures are kind of pointless, everything I learned was from the textbook which he straight up teaches from in lecture. He doesn't record lectures or give much practice though which sucks because that's the best way to understand the material. His exams were hard but make sure you look at his practice exams, they're super helpful. The reason I give 2 stars is because I felt like I was my own teacher and Isaacs himself contributed nothing to learning or studying. But if you believe you can make time for this class every week and not just right before an exam you should get an A. A 50% is a guaranteed C and 80% is an A (not minus). But his final was so cooked that he curved a little extra and my 74% turned into an A-, so do what you will with that info. This class is mostly memorizing reactions and when to use them, it's lowkey not that bad it's just a LOT of reactions, so the more time you spend on the material the easier it becomes.

I wish no bad feelings toward Dr. Isaacs. 
That being said, the current rating is too high/deceiving. Dr. Isaacs does put in some effort, but honestly, it seems minimal. The slides are mostly just reactions and mechanisms with barely any explanation or details we actually need for the exams. I get that we’re supposed to take notes ourselves, but there’s not much space on the slides, and he flies through the material fast that it’s easy to miss key points. He didn’t post most of the lectures, and there were only two midterms plus a ridiculously long final exam which means if you mess up one exam, you're cooked.
The content is the usual overwhelming amount to memorize, which is typical for organic chemistry, but he adds more unnecessary information we need to know. For example, the nomenclature section on exams often required memorizing how to draw random molecules from scratch (and he wouldnt just tell us which 20 we should know…he would take random ones from the notes or book). This distracts from the important concepts we should focus on, and it doesn’t help for things like the MCAT either. I bet everyone has already forgotten them by now anyway.
Not that this is unfair, but just a warning: there are already tons of reactions and mechanisms to learn, and he throws in tricky questions that require knowing minor details or exceptions about them. 

Exams are very difficult. The second exam was the only one that was reasonable in my opinion. Our final was the first year he did it in multiple choice format, and it felt harder due to the sheer number of questions and options. A lot of us ran out of time and had to guess on many questions. I would’ve much preferred fewer questions that required written answers. Also not that this was a big deal, but he lowkey abandoned us on finals day.

Overall, Dr. Isaacs doesn’t teach as if students are learning the material for the first time. You’ll have to teach yourself or go to TA hours like everyday, which makes it very difficult to balance with other classes. Dr. isaacs section ended up being way more time-consuming and difficult than I expected, and I thought I knew what to expect after orgo 1. I don’t want to be too harsh, but it felt like everything was on us, and if we did badly, it was made out to always be our fault…but he could’ve done more such as review common issues/problems/concepts students struggle with on exams more frequently, provide more practice problems for the final, send out helpful advice and resources to the class, etc. I did appreciate him holding review sessions and trying to make the times available for everyone, but they were canceled many times and did not help much. At one point I just read the textbook like he told us to and did well, but it took so much time to do that +take notes + practice (i spent 140 hours studying for finals and passed) and I did not have the hours to do that for the entire semester. 

Also, just look at the withdrawal rate…it’s clearly not normal. The curve was large, but I think we should’ve gotten at least a slightly bigger curve, given the new final format and how low the average was. He also needs to add more graded assignments since the three exams are all that count. One bad day and you will be forced to drop. He’s not a bad lecturer and can explain things well, but other chemistry professors I had put in much more effort and care with their teaching methods, course materials, and helping their students succeed. 

Expect much sacrifice or suffering if you take this professor. I’m not exaggerating.

Awesome guy. I’m so glad I ended up with him even though I tried so hard to get Davis. His exams are so straightforward and just like the practice exams. He never gives trick questions and you’ll pretty much ace every exam if you attend lectures, because that’s when he tells you exactly what he’s putting on them. I had it so much better than people taking other professors, I would def recommend!!
Nice professor but I wish he has homework or worksheets for completion to give a better buffer for exams.

As many of the reviews say, Isaacs is a nice guy, and you can tell he genuinely loves chemistry which is nice, but as a professor, do not take him unless you absolutely have to. I took him because it was the only Orgo II which fit in my schedule, and seeing previous reviews that an 80 was the requirement for an A, I thought it wouldn't be too bad, but boy was I wrong. Keep in mind, I got an A in Orgo I with a normal amount of studying. On the first exam, I got a 67% (lol), the lowest grade of my life, and I genuinely thought I was stupid because I did put in a lot of time to study for the exam. Even with that low of a grade it was still higher than about 75% of the class, which goes to show how difficult his exams are. The type of questions on the exams that you would think, "oh he wouldn't put that on the exam," he put on the exams. The second midterm I did significantly better on because I put a crazy amount of studying into it, weeks in advance, and honestly the second midterm was a lot more realistic than the first one. The final, I genuinely walked out of thinking I failed. It was the MCQ final, which, for orgo, is not a good idea because there is no chance for partial credit. Somehow, I managed to do well on that, which got me right above the 80% threshold to get an A, but it was a mix of luck and good guessing skills, not due to any of the studying I did. To do well in this class, I recommend watching videos on the mechanisms he requires, memorizing them, doing all of his past exams, attending discussions and GSS if you can, and just putting in a lot of time. He does teach exactly from the textbook, so if that helps you, read it; if not, at least skim the textbook problems. I don't learn well from textbooks, so I watched videos about the topics instead of reading. If I could take this class again, I would not take it with Isaacs, and I am sure it would have been a much less stressful semester.

The reviews of Dr. Wang's teaching style and exams are pretty accurate. He basically reads off slides that are copied and pasted from the textbook that you have access too so going to lecture is not really necessary (I went around 5 times the whole semester and ended with an A-). This definitely means you need to teach yourself the majority of the information, but it's honestly not that bad since all the material is the same concept throughout the semester. I would say that going to class is somewhat beneficial since he does do synthesis practice problems that are guaranteed to be on the exam, so I would consider going just for that. 

Regarding the structure of the class, it was two midterms (150 points each) and a final (250 points), with no graded homework, clicker points, or anything else. So, going into the semester, I was definitely worried about that, but he literally tells you everything on the exam during review days. He makes a list of the reaction conditions, mechanisms, synthesis, and theory concepts on the exam. So as long as you study and check off everything on that list, you'll be fine. 

The actual content on the exams is essentially a copy and paste from the practice exams he gives you (he also gives you keys to the practice exams). Every exam is formatted the same, with concept/theory first, then reaction conditions, then mechanism, and finally synthesis. You're never blindsighted on question format on the exams, so as long as you study what he tells you, do the practice exam, then the exams will feel very familiar. I will say that exams are pretty lengthy (usually around 10-12 pages), but they are 100% doable in the time he gives you (I have 1.5 exam time and I always finished within the regular time given).

Dr. Wang himself is very caring for his students. He always answers questions with a smile on his face and makes sure you understand before leaving his office. One note I do have is that he is not very technologically advanced, so sometimes during the lecture, his camera, which projected the paper he wrote on for practice problems, wouldn't always work, and he doesn't notice, so sometimes you just need to accept that you aren't going to be able to write that problem down. But I don't really have anything negative to say other than that this is kind of a teach yourself type of course. I would recommend taking him if you do not have a problem with putting in effort outside of class time.
bad, should be a 3 stars. i would take a diff professor. exam questions came out of no where.

Only complaint is a thick accent. The best thing IMO is that the content on the exam is very clear and transparent. Know the slides, and learn the specific mechanisms stated on the content & review slides and you're set. Practice exams were damn near 95% similar in structure and format to the actual exams. The final is pretty hard as it is cumulative and you end up learning quite a lot but thats expected. There were some hard specifics/nuance questions like "which intermediary steps would you expect in acid/basic conds." that require you to know the mechanisms super well but these were very few compared to the bs I experienced in prof. Dixon's class. I missed quite a few of em but still got 80's on the exams. Took class in Fall '25.

took CHEM231 with her last semester, and I’m taking CHEM241 with her right now (Spring 2026). my review for that class starts with “Take her!” for reference.

there’s a lot of good in this class --- everything I mentioned in my 231 review, in fact. She still brings her love of the game and continues to connect new topics to familiar ones in a way that just works.

there’s not much else to add beyond what I wrote there. I’d just recommend making a basic Anki deck for mechanisms on an exam-by-exam basis and continue to review those to stay fresh for synthesis problems.

TL;DR: This class is awesome. Dr. Koppel is awesome. Take her class.
